channel.title: Comments on: Religion… an Opiate?
channel.description: taoism, taoist thought, buddha, yoga, tai chi, shakuhachi

item.title: By: Carl Abbott
item.dc:creator: Carl Abbott
item.description:
Chapter 36 indicates that all is "in harmony with the Tao". It is just a matter of which phase we need or fear to see. Phases being: fullness v. emptiness, life v. death, conflict v. resolution, discord v. harmony, etc., or as chapter 36 puts it,
<a href="https://centertao.local/tao-te-ching/carl/chapter-36/" rel="nofollow">In desiring weakness, one must first strive. In desiring to let go, one must first begin. In desiring to get, one must first give.</a>.
Of course, this is the story I want (need) to hear. I find it more comforting to see both sides of the coin. Thus, the idea of "eliminating" anything feels somewhat fanciful, i.e., something and nothing produce each other, or as chapter 2 puts it, <a href="https://centertao.local/tao-te-ching/carl/chapter-2/" rel="nofollow">Hence existence and nothing give birth to one another</a>.
In the final analysis, isn't this all "mental speculation". Thought, and the language (words and names) that expresses it, is mental. As I see it, we are all trying to find a way to think about what we experience that 'harmonizes' with our experience. This odd, ironic mirror quality of 'mind only' is in the end irrational because, in the end, our emotions (fears and needs) drive mental activity (thought). So, we just stumble along, <a href="https://centertao.local/2011/09/09/strive-on-diligently/" rel="nofollow">striving on diligently</a> trying to do the best we can.

In desiring weakness, one must first strive.
In desiring to let go, one must first begin.
In desiring to get, one must first give..

Of course, this is the story I want (need) to hear. I find it more comforting to see both sides of the coin. Thus, the idea of “eliminating” anything feels somewhat fanciful, i.e., something and nothing produce each other, or as chapter 2 puts it, Hence existence and nothing give birth to one another.

In the final analysis, isn’t this all “mental speculation”. Thought, and the language (words and names) that expresses it, is mental. As I see it, we are all trying to find a way to think about what we experience that ‘harmonizes’ with our experience. This odd, ironic mirror quality of ‘mind only’ is in the end irrational because, in the end, our emotions (fears and needs) drive mental activity (thought). So, we just stumble along, striving on diligently trying to do the best we can.

item.title: By: Carl Abbott
item.dc:creator: Carl Abbott
item.description:
The "mental box" is of our own making. To say religion is an opiate is looking at this from the inside out, and failing to realize that the 'out' we are seeing is simply a reflection of the 'inside' (our own personal fears and needs).
In other words, the "mental box" is simply failing to realize I don't know: <a href="https://centertao.local/tao-te-ching/carl/chapter-71/" rel="nofollow">Realizing I don’t know is better; not knowing this knowing is disease</a>.
"Elimination of any metal box" would be a lobotomy, which would make one appear to "be in harmony with the Tao". ;-)
item.content:encoded:
The “mental box” is of our own making. To say religion is an opiate is looking at this from the inside out, and failing to realize that the ‘out’ we are seeing is simply a reflection of the ‘inside’ (our own personal fears and needs).

In other words, the “mental box” is simply failing to realize I don’t know: Realizing I don’t know is better; not knowing this knowing is disease.

“Elimination of any metal box” would be a lobotomy, which would make one appear to “be in harmony with the Tao”. 😉
